t: Amenorrhea, abnormal bleeding, PCOS and female infertility
sub: Rule out pregnancy, then find the failing level: hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary or outflow tract. The same logic sorts bleeding, PCOS and infertility.

pretest.q: What is the first test in any woman with amenorrhea?
pretest.why: Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea, so an hCG test comes first, even when she reports no sexual activity. Prolactin, TSH and FSH come next to localize the failing level.

w.Serum prolactin: Prolactin belongs to the second step with TSH and FSH. Pregnancy itself raises prolactin, so testing it before hCG can mislead.
w.Serum FSH: FSH separates ovarian failure from brain causes, but only after a negative hCG has excluded pregnancy.
w.Pelvic MRI: Imaging is reserved for specific questions, such as a suspected pituitary mass or unclear anatomy. It is never the opening test.

pretest.q: Which drug is first-line for inducing ovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome?
pretest.why: Letrozole inhibits aromatase, so estrogen feedback falls and FSH rises enough to grow a follicle. In PCOS it gives more live births than clomiphene, the older alternative.

w.Spironolactone: Spironolactone blocks androgen receptors to treat hirsutism. It does not induce ovulation, and it is stopped before conception because it can feminize a male fetus.
w.Cabergoline: Cabergoline is a dopamine agonist that restores ovulation in hyperprolactinemia, a different cause of anovulation with normal androgens.
w.Leuprolide: Continuous leuprolide downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors and shuts ovulation off. It treats endometriosis and precocious puberty.

body: What counts as amenorrhea, and what comes first?

Amenorrhea is the absence of menses. **Primary amenorrhea** means no menarche by age 15 when breast development is normal. It also means no menarche by age 13 when there is no breast development at all. **Secondary amenorrhea** means no menses for 3 months in a woman who had regular cycles, or for 6 months after irregular ones. Pregnancy is the most common cause. So a pregnancy test for human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) comes first in every case, even when she reports no sexual activity. Lactation and menopause also stop periods normally.

In primary amenorrhea, two exam findings sort the causes. Breasts show that estrogen has been made, and a uterus shows that the Müllerian ducts developed. A girl without breasts lacks estrogen. A high follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) means **hypergonadotropic** hypogonadism, in which the gonad has failed, as in Turner syndrome, the most common cause of primary amenorrhea. A karyotype confirms it. A low FSH means **hypogonadotropic** hypogonadism, in which the failure lies above the ovary, as in constitutional delay or **Kallmann syndrome**. In Kallmann syndrome, GnRH neurons fail to migrate with olfactory neurons, so anosmia results. Breasts without a uterus mean Müllerian agenesis with vaginal agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, 46,XX) or complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY).

Breasts and a uterus point either to an outflow block or to the same causes as secondary amenorrhea, which are then worked up the same way. In an outflow block, an **imperforate hymen** or a transverse vaginal septum traps menstrual blood behind it. Over months the vagina fills, a state called {{rp9_hemato|hematocolpos}}. The girl has cyclic pelvic pain, a bulging bluish membrane and a lower-abdominal mass, sometimes with urinary retention. Incising the membrane cures it.

Primary and secondary amenorrhea share one logic: find the failing level. The classic scheme uses {{rp9_compart|four compartments}}. Compartment I is the uterus and outflow tract, II is the ovary, III is the anterior pituitary and IV is the hypothalamus. Failure in II gives a high FSH (hypergonadotropic). Failure in III or IV gives a low FSH and LH (hypogonadotropic). Failure in I leaves the hormones normal.
How do three blood tests localize secondary amenorrhea?

Once hCG is negative, measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), prolactin and FSH. **Prolactin** suppresses GnRH pulses, so a high level lowers FSH and LH. Causes include a prolactinoma, dopamine-blocking drugs and hypothyroidism, because high TRH also stimulates prolactin. A high prolactin with no drug or thyroid cause calls for a pituitary MRI. A high FSH on two occasions before age 40 means ovarian failure. A low or normal FSH with low estradiol puts the failure above the ovary. Examples are {{rp9_fha|functional hypothalamic amenorrhea}}, Sheehan syndrome, Cushing syndrome and an empty sella. Normal results suggest PCOS when androgens are high, or Asherman syndrome after curettage.

{{rp9_poi|Primary ovarian insufficiency}} means the follicles stop working before age 40. The woman has amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea and a low estradiol that causes hot flashes and vaginal dryness. Her FSH is in the menopausal range on two samples at least a month apart. Without follicles, no estradiol or inhibin restrains the pituitary, so FSH is high. Causes include alkylating chemotherapy such as cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiation, a fragile X premutation, autoimmune oophoritis, Turner syndrome and, often, no cause found. A karyotype and FMR1 testing look for the genetic causes.
A withdrawal bleed proves estrogen and an open outflow tract

In a **progestin challenge**, the woman takes a progestin for 7 to 10 days and then stops. A withdrawal bleed means estrogen had already built an endometrium and blood can escape, so the problem is anovulation, as in PCOS. No bleed means estrogen is low or outflow is blocked. If estrogen plus progestin still gives no bleed, the uterus or outflow tract is at fault.

Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea follows weight loss, intense exercise or stress, with or without **disordered eating**. Low energy availability lowers leptin and raises cortisol, which slows GnRH pulses, so FSH, LH and estradiol all fall. The **female athlete triad** links low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density, because estrogen normally restrains bone resorption. Stress fractures follow. The newer term, relative energy deficiency in sport, also covers thyroid, immune and cardiac effects and male athletes. Treatment restores energy intake, because a birth control pill brings back bleeding but does not repair bone.
Normal hormones do not rule out a uterine cause

After a postpartum or post-abortion curettage, a woman may stop menstruating because the basalis was scraped away and adhesions formed. This is Asherman syndrome. Her FSH, prolactin, TSH and estradiol are normal and she still ovulates, so the labs look reassuring. The history is the clue, and hysteroscopy is the proof. In Sheehan syndrome, by contrast, the pituitary that enlarged in pregnancy outgrows its blood supply and infarcts after a hemorrhage, so lactation fails first.
Why does PCOS cause anovulation, androgen excess and endometrial risk?

In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), GnRH pulses run fast, which favors LH over FSH. LH drives {{rp8_theca|theca cells}} to make more androgen. **Insulin resistance** adds to this. High insulin stimulates theca cells directly. It also lowers the liver's output of {{rp9_shbg|sex hormone-binding globulin}} (SHBG), so **free testosterone** rises even when total testosterone is only mildly high. Low FSH and local androgen stall follicles at the small antral stage, so many small follicles line the enlarged ovary (the string of pearls on ultrasound) and none becomes dominant. Without ovulation there is no corpus luteum and no progesterone, so the endometrium meets **unopposed estrogen**, including estrone made by aromatase in fat. This is why PCOS raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, infertility and type 2 diabetes.

The {{rp9_rotterdam|Rotterdam criteria}} diagnose PCOS when two of three findings are present: oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia and nonclassic **congenital adrenal hyperplasia** (high 17-hydroxyprogesterone) must be excluded first. Losing 5 to 10 percent of body weight can restore ovulation. A combined oral contraceptive suppresses LH, raises SHBG and protects the endometrium, and cyclic progestin protects it when a pill is not wanted. Metformin treats insulin resistance. **Spironolactone** blocks androgen receptors to treat hirsutism, with contraception because it can feminize a male fetus. For fertility, **letrozole** is first-line.
Which other endocrine disorders stop periods or add androgen?

Disease outside the ovary stops periods by several routes. Excess prolactin or cortisol suppresses GnRH, excess androgen blocks follicle maturation, and excess estrone made in fat feeds back on the pituitary. Loss of pituitary function does the same. An **empty sella**, a sella turcica filled with cerebrospinal fluid that flattens the pituitary, usually leaves hormones normal. A squeezed gland can still cause a low FSH and LH, and a squeezed stalk removes dopamine's restraint on prolactin.
Why periods stop or androgen rises
Fat makes estrone, and insulin drives ovarian androgen, so ovulation fails
In hypothyroidism, high TRH raises prolactin, which suppresses GnRH; thyrotoxicosis also disrupts cycles
Goiter, temperature intolerance; abnormal TSH, high prolactin
21-hydroxylase deficiency shunts steroid into adrenal androgen
Cortisol excess suppresses GnRH and adds adrenal androgen
Striae, central obesity; high late-night salivary cortisol
Fast-onset virilization means a tumor until proven otherwise

PCOS hirsutism starts around puberty and progresses slowly. Rapid onset or **virilization**, such as clitoromegaly, a deepening voice and temporal balding, suggests an androgen-secreting tumor. Very high testosterone with a normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (**DHEA-S**) points to an ovarian tumor. A very high DHEA-S points to an adrenal tumor, because DHEA-S comes almost entirely from the adrenal cortex.
How is abnormal uterine bleeding named and sorted?

**Heavy menstrual bleeding**, once called menorrhagia, means more than 80 mL of blood lost per cycle or periods longer than 7 days. Intermenstrual bleeding, once metrorrhagia, falls between regular periods, and menometrorrhagia is heavy and irregular. Oligomenorrhea means cycles longer than 35 days, and polymenorrhea means cycles shorter than 21 days. **Postmenopausal bleeding** is any bleeding 12 months or more after the final period, and it is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.

First confirm that the blood comes from the uterus, and exclude pregnancy with hCG. Abnormal uterine bleeding is then sorted with {{rp9_palm|PALM-COEIN}}: four structural causes seen on imaging or histology and five nonstructural ones. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first image. Endometrial biopsy is added when cancer is a concern, such as from age 45, or earlier with obesity or PCOS.
Intermenstrual spotting; focal mass on ultrasound
Heavy, painful periods; enlarged boggy uterus
Heavy bleeding; firm, irregular enlarged uterus
Postmenopausal bleeding or long unopposed estrogen
Heavy bleeding since menarche; von Willebrand disease
Regular cycles with a local hemostasis defect

Ovulatory dysfunction is the most common nonstructural cause. Without a corpus luteum, estrogen builds a thick, fragile lining that no progesterone stabilizes, so it breaks down in patches. It is common just after menarche, when the LH surge is not yet reliable. It is also common in perimenopause, when a dwindling follicle pool lowers estradiol and inhibin B, FSH rises and cycles turn irregular and anovulatory.
Which pelvic changes cause pain, cysts and infertility?

**Primary dysmenorrhea** begins within a year or two of menarche, once cycles are ovulatory. The secretory endometrium releases prostaglandins, mainly PGF2α, which cause strong uterine contractions and ischemia, so NSAIDs are first-line. Secondary dysmenorrhea has a pelvic cause, such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids or adhesions after pelvic infection.

In **endometriosis**, endometrial glands and stroma grow outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas. Retrograde menstruation carries tissue there, and the implants respond to estrogen: they bleed each cycle and cause inflammation and scarring. Bleeding into an ovary forms an **endometrioma**, a cyst of old brown blood. Repeated bleeding and healing bind pelvic organs together as **pelvic adhesions**, which distort the tubes and ovaries and cause infertility. Pain is cyclic: dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia and, with bowel involvement, painful defecation (dyschezia). Ultrasound shows an endometrioma, but only laparoscopy shows small implants and gives tissue proof. Treatment is NSAIDs plus estrogen suppression with hormonal contraceptives, progestins or GnRH agonists.

A **follicular cyst** is the simplest structural change in ovulation: a follicle that never ruptures keeps filling with fluid beyond 3 cm. It is thin walled, usually painless and resolves within a few cycles, although a large cyst can rupture or twist the ovary. In PCOS, by contrast, many small follicles stall and no single cyst forms.
What are premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder?

**Premenstrual syndrome** is a cluster of mood and physical symptoms, such as irritability, bloating and breast tenderness, that appear in the luteal week and ease within a few days of menses. It occurs only in ovulatory cycles. The severe mood form, **premenstrual dysphoric disorder** (PMDD), disrupts daily life and is treated first with an SSRI. A combined hormonal contraceptive also helps because it stops ovulation.
How is infertility defined, investigated and treated?

Infertility is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. At age 35 or older, 6 months is enough, because fertility falls with maternal age. **Primary infertility** means no prior pregnancy, and secondary infertility follows at least one. Both partners are evaluated. A semen analysis checks the male side, where a varicocele is a common treatable cause. For the woman, regular cycles and a mid-luteal progesterone confirm ovulation, and AMH and the antral follicle count estimate ovarian reserve. Risk factors in women are age, pelvic inflammatory disease (which scars the tubes), endometriosis, PCOS, obesity and smoking. In men they are varicocele, undescended testes, heat and gonadotoxic drugs.

{{rp9_hsg|Hysterosalpingography}} pushes contrast through the cervix to outline the cavity and tubes. Free spill into the peritoneum proves tubal **patency**. A blocked, fluid-filled hydrosalpinx dilates and shows no spill. A **filling defect** inside the cavity means something occupies it, such as a polyp, a submucosal fibroid, the adhesions of Asherman syndrome or a clot.

Ovulation induction uses letrozole or clomiphene. Intrauterine insemination suits mild male factor or unexplained infertility with open tubes. In vitro fertilization bypasses blocked tubes: gonadotropins stimulate several follicles, an hCG trigger matures the eggs, and the eggs are retrieved, fertilized and transferred. For severe male factor, {{rp9_icsi|intracytoplasmic sperm injection}} places one sperm in each egg, with surgical **sperm retrieval** when the ejaculate holds no sperm.
How letrozole and clomiphene make a follicle grow
Letrozole inhibits **aromatase**, so estradiol falls. Clomiphene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, blocks hypothalamic estrogen receptors. Either way, negative feedback is removed.
The hypothalamus speeds GnRH pulses, and the pituitary releases more FSH and LH. This rescues a follicle from atresia.
Estradiol from the growing follicle triggers an LH surge, or an hCG injection acting on LH receptors is timed to trigger ovulation.

More than one follicle can ovulate, causing twins. Injected gonadotropins with an hCG trigger can cause **ovarian hyperstimulation** syndrome, with enlarged ovaries and leaky capillaries that cause ascites and clotting.
Why can clomiphene, a drug that blocks estrogen receptors, cause ovulation?

The hypothalamus reads the block as a lack of estrogen, so it speeds GnRH pulses and the pituitary releases more FSH and LH. The extra FSH grows follicles, and the dominant follicle's rising estradiol then triggers an LH surge. The same blockade explains the side effects. Central receptor blockade causes hot flashes and visual changes, and blockade in the endometrium and cervix causes a thin endometrium and thick cervical mucus.

body.q: A 24-year-old with 8 months of amenorrhea, a negative hCG and normal TSH and prolactin bleeds after a progestin challenge. Which reasoning is best?
o: Bleeding proves ovarian failure, because only a high FSH primes the endometrium
Bleeding means estrogen primed the lining and the outflow tract is open, so she is not ovulating
Bleeding means the endometrium is scarred and bleeds when progesterone stops
Bleeding means her hypothalamus is suppressed and estradiol is high
body.why: Progestin withdrawal causes bleeding only if estrogen has already built an endometrium and blood has a way out. A positive challenge therefore places her problem at ovulation: she makes estrogen but forms no corpus luteum, so no progesterone. PCOS is the classic cause. Ovarian failure and hypothalamic suppression both leave estrogen low, and Asherman scarring would prevent bleeding altogether.

grid.q: Which of these point to polycystic ovary syndrome?
items: Cycles every 45 to 90 days since menarche
High free testosterone with low SHBG
Many small antral follicles on ultrasound
Proliferative endometrium late in the cycle
Withdrawal bleed after a progestin challenge
Very high DHEA-S with rapid virilization
Bulging bluish hymen with cyclic pelvic pain
